solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Popular line-up

parts.note: something popular is said to be in
a crease is a line, as on a trouser leg or in cricket

explanation.surface: A chart-topping band or a well-liked team selection.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen tempts you to read 'line-up' as one word; split it, and 'up' is a verb, as in to up the price.
explanation.definitionFit: To up something is to raise it, so the verb and the answer are synonyms.

clue.text: Nice move securing instant rise in salary

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading from the bottom upwards, so the letters go backwards
to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece is held inside another
to move letters is to shift them about into a different arrangement

parts.note: the French city's name, used as letters
a mo is a moment, short for 'moment'

explanation.surface: Someone moving to Nice gets an immediate pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice move' reads like praise or a relocation to the French Riviera, and 'rise in salary' like the definition; but 'rise' turns its piece upside down in a down clue, leaving 'salary' alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A salary is the money a person earns from a job, which is their regular earnings.

clue.text: With spicy dish not suitable for all, man's brought in fruit

indicators.note: something brought in is taken inside, so one piece goes within another
saying 'not' some quality strips it out, so those letters are removed

parts.note: a curry is a spicy dish
U is the British film certificate meaning suitable for all ages
a man is 'he'; the 's is 'has'

explanation.surface: A man arrives with a fruit to go with a curry too fiery for everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a U-certificate film is suitable for all audiences, so U leaves CURRY, and HE goes into what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherry is a small stone fruit, so the answer is one example of the category.

clue.text: What about paintings by Lowry — ultimately unsophisticated?

indicators.note: to be about something is to go around it, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: 'eh?' is what you say when you mean 'what?'
paintings are art

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of Lowry

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether L. S. Lowry's matchstick-figure paintings are, in the end, rather naive.
explanation.walkthrough: L. S. Lowry was an English painter of industrial northern towns; his name only supplies its last letter, and 'ultimately' belongs to the wordplay, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy humour or tastes are coarse, plain and down-to-earth, the opposite of refined or worldly.

clue.text: Team grabs pole before second of advantage wasted

indicators.note: to grab something is to clutch it, so one piece holds another inside

parts.note: a squad is a sports team
N stands for the north pole
ere is an old word for before

indicators.note: the second of a word means its second letter only

parts.note: the second letter of advantage

explanation.surface: A racing team takes pole position, only to throw away its edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' looks like a positional link, but here it supplies the old word ERE, which sits between the team holding N and the final D.
explanation.definitionFit: To squander money or chances is to waste them carelessly, so both past-tense verbs match.

clue.text: Glad judge has zero qualms finally imprisoning second person

indicators.note: to imprison is to lock inside, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for judge
zero looks like the letter O
'you' is the second-person pronoun

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the last letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of qualms

explanation.surface: A judge is happy to have no qualms about jailing a second offender.
explanation.walkthrough: O and S together hold YOU, all after J; 'second person' is grammar, not a second criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyous means full of joy, a close synonym for being happy or pleased.

clue.text: Record AI breaking into work with traditional art material

indicators.note: something breaking falls apart, and its pieces can be put together anew
to work material is to knead and reshape it, as a potter does with clay

parts.note: an LP is a long-playing record
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Artificial intelligence breaks into art, setting a record for work done in an old medium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' looks like a link meaning entry, but its letters join LP and AI in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil paint, pigment ground in linseed oil, has been the standard medium of easel painters for centuries.

clue.text: Sometimes old granny gets day out

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
nan is a familiar British word for a grandmother
D is the abbreviation for day
a light that is out is off

explanation.surface: Every so often, an elderly grandmother gets a day trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Day out' reads as an outing; it splits into D and OFF.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something on and off means doing it intermittently, which is to say occasionally rather than constantly.

clue.text: Watch small cat maybe caught inside a hollow tree

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small

indicators.note: being inside means sitting within, so one piece is placed in another

parts.note: a cat is one example of a pet, as 'maybe' signals
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
taken as written

indicators.note: a hollow thing has nothing in the middle, so only the outer letters remain

parts.note: the outside letters of tree

explanation.surface: Look out for a little cat that may be stuck in a hollow tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' sounds like an order to observe the cat, and is the definition; C goes inside PET, after S, before A and the shell of tree.
explanation.definitionFit: To spectate is to look on as a member of an audience, which is what watching an event means.

clue.text: Hurrah! Drink lifts the spirits

parts.note: a hurrah is a cheer; plural here
to sup is to drink; the S is borrowed from the cheer

explanation.surface: A toast: a drink raises everyone's mood, with 'spirits' hinting at the liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters split differently from the enumeration: the S belongs to the drink, not the hurrah, and 'sup' is an old word for sipping.
explanation.definitionFit: To cheer someone up is to make them happier, which is exactly raising their mood or morale.

clue.text: Chef regularly overcooked veal chop

indicators.note: food that is overcooked has broken down and lost its shape
regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: first and third letters of Chef
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook who habitually overdoes the veal chops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Veal chop' reads as a cut of meat, but 'chop' is a verb and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To cleave is to split something with a heavy blow, as a butcher does with a cleaver.

clue.text: Trader encountered fencing round restructured ranch

indicators.note: a fence runs round a space, enclosing what lies within

parts.note: to have encountered someone is to have met them

indicators.note: something restructured has been reorganised into a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dealer comes across someone putting a fence round a reorganised ranch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fencing' fits the ranch picture, but here it means enclosing, with 'round' completing the signal rather than describing the fence.
explanation.definitionFit: A merchant buys and sells goods for profit, so the two words name the same occupation.

clue.text: Evacuated neighbourhood inspires temptation for robber

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one piece takes another inside

parts.note: bait is a lure or temptation

indicators.note: an evacuated place has been emptied, so only its outer letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of neighbourhood

explanation.surface: An empty district tempts a burglar.
explanation.walkthrough: BAIT takes in the shell of neighbourhood.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandit is an outlaw who robs people, typically by force, so the answer names a kind of thief.

clue.text: Finished fine gold bags, now available

parts.note: when time is up it is finished
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
or is gold in heraldry
to bag something is to grab it

explanation.surface: Fine gold handbags, newly made, are on sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' looks like a noun for handbags but works as a verb: to bag is to seize.
explanation.definitionFit: Something up for grabs is there for anyone to take, so it is open and obtainable at present.

clue.text: Working out reportedly essential code with which gift's ordered

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we go by the sound

parts.note: a key PIN is a vital personal identification number

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, here into a fresh sequence

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone works out the vital code needed to order a present online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working out' looks like cracking the code, but it is the definition, as in exercise. A PIN is a personal identification number, and a key one is essential.
explanation.definitionFit: Working out at the gym is exercising, and keeping fit is the everyday phrase for regular physical exercise.

clue.text: Awful hotel's boiler repair overruns

parts.note: H is the NATO phonetic alphabet's letter for hotel

indicators.note: a repair takes apart and puts back together, so the letters are reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs, set over (above) the rest

explanation.surface: A bad hotel complains that the boiler repair is running late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overruns' looks like a delay, but splits as over plus runs: R from cricket joins BOILER in the jumble, after H.
explanation.definitionFit: Awful and horrible are close synonyms, both meaning very bad or unpleasant.

clue.text: Saved uncovered spring wheat ahead of inclement weather

indicators.note: to spring is to leap about, so the letters jump into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: with its covering taken off, a word loses its outermost letters

parts.note: Saved without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A farmer rescues the spring wheat crop before bad weather arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring wheat' is a real crop, so 'spring' hides as an adjective; the jumbled WHEAT comes ahead of the core of Saved.
explanation.definitionFit: Inclement weather is harsh or unpleasant weather; a spell of extreme heat counts as one kind of it.

clue.text: Sets up positions on wetlands

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to fit something is to position it in place
fens are low marshy lands, as in eastern England

explanation.surface: Someone establishes positions out on the marshes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sets up' looks like one phrasal verb; split it, so 'Sets' is the definition and 'up' turns FITS round.
explanation.definitionFit: When jelly or cement sets it becomes firm and rigid, which is to say it hardens.

clue.text: Open to ambassador stopping President going too far

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so one piece fills a space within the others

parts.note: overt means open, not hidden
an ambassador is addressed as His Excellency, HE
taken as written
P is the abbreviation for President

explanation.surface: An envoy openly blocks a president who is exceeding his powers.
explanation.walkthrough: An ambassador is styled His Excellency, a title crosswords shorten to its initials; 'to' is used as it stands.
explanation.definitionFit: Over-the-top describes behaviour that is excessive or exaggerated, beyond reasonable limits.

clue.text: Try to find water that's holy?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to search for underground water with a dowsing rod

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark invites you to think of holy water; the verb sense is dowsing, the adjective sense is godly.
explanation.definitionFit: Dowsers are said to divine water, and anything of or from God is described as sacred in this sense.

clue.text: Discontinue introduction of digs on building sites

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of digs

indicators.note: building means constructing, putting materials together into a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An order to stop starting excavations on construction sites.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Building sites' is a ready-made phrase, which hides 'building' as the signal to rework SITES; in a down clue D sits on top.
explanation.definitionFit: To desist is to cease doing something, so it is a formal synonym for stopping an activity.

clue.text: Value of company when fixed by dollar

parts.note: 'as' can mean when, as in 'as I left'
something fixed is set
S is the shape behind the dollar sign

explanation.surface: A firm's valuation, set against the dollar exchange rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed by dollar' sounds like currency pegging, but splits into SET and S.
explanation.definitionFit: A company's assets are everything it owns of worth, which together make up what the business is worth.

clue.text: Confirm if a try's converted

indicators.note: converting something changes it into a different form

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe-s

explanation.surface: A rugby question: confirm whether the try has been converted.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby a try is converted by kicking it between the posts for extra points; here 'converted' just changes the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To ratify a treaty or decision is to approve it formally, giving it official confirmation.

clue.text: Grotesque quality of government policies in America

indicators.note: being in something means sitting within it, so these pieces go inside

parts.note: US is the United States
G is the abbreviation for government
a party line is a policy

explanation.surface: A complaint about the monstrous nature of American government policy.
explanation.walkthrough: A party line is its official policy, so 'policies' can be lines; 'quality' belongs with 'Grotesque' in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something grotesque is distorted and hideous, so its defining characteristic is extreme unsightliness.

clue.text: Cheeky underwear and top reduced by 50%

indicators.note: cutting something by fifty per cent leaves only half of it

parts.note: a bra is an item of underwear
the zenith is the highest point, the top

explanation.surface: A cheeky sale: underwear and tops at half price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like a garment beside the underwear, but it means the highest point, ZENITH, of which only the first half is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Brazen behaviour is bold and shameless, much like impudent or saucy behaviour.

clue.text: Make the most of Miami trip including times by shore on vacation

indicators.note: to include something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside
to trip is to stumble, and stumbling letters fall out of order

parts.note: taken as written
x is the multiplication sign, read as 'times'

indicators.note: a place on vacation is left empty, so just the outer letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of shore

explanation.surface: Get the most out of a Miami holiday by spending time on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trip' and 'vacation' both fit a holiday, but each is a signal. MIAMI rearranged holds X, then the empty shore follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To maximise something is to get as much from it as possible, which is the phrase's exact sense.

clue.text: Free verse's prose at heart really

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and can rearrange

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letter is taken

parts.note: the middle letter of prose

explanation.surface: A literary claim that free verse is really just prose underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free verse' is a genuine term for unrhymed poetry, so 'Free' hides as part of it; VERSE rearranged gains the centre of prose.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever so is an informal intensifier, as in 'ever so kind', meaning very or extremely.

clue.text: A most piercing cry for help to contain toxic stuff

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to pierce something is to go into it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: SOS is the distress signal
the most, in the sense of the greatest, is the best

explanation.surface: A shrill scream for help about containing a hazardous substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piercing cry' reads as a loud scream, but 'piercing' is the signal, and 'most' means the best rather than very.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestos is a fibrous mineral once used in insulation, now known to cause lung disease when inhaled.
